new_entities.name: Pediatric adenotonsillectomy for obstructive sleep apnea
new_entities.description: Adenotonsillectomy performed in children with obstructive sleep apnea or sleep-disordered breathing.

new_entities.name: Clinical outcomes
new_entities.description: Overall clinical, sleep-related, behavioral, cardiovascular, and quality-of-life outcomes after an intervention.

edges.effect_quant: Adenotonsillectomy improves many pediatric OSA outcomes, but benefit varies by age and severity. A 2023 meta-analysis of 93 studies found better disease and comorbidity improvement when surgery occurred between ages 3 and 7, while randomized trials showed stronger gains in quality of life, symptoms, and reduced progression than in executive-function primary endpoints.
edges.population: children with uncomplicated obstructive sleep apnea or clinically important sleep-disordered breathing, especially preschool and school-age children with adenotonsillar hypertrophy
edges.mechanism: Removing hypertrophied tonsils and adenoids enlarges the upper airway, decreases obstructive events, improves oxygenation and sleep continuity, and can relieve downstream behavioral and cardiovascular strain.
edges.summary: This is generally a protective edge, but it is not uniformly curative. The strongest benefits are seen in symptom burden, quality of life, and physiologic disease severity, while neurocognitive primary outcomes in milder disease can be less dramatic.
edges.caveats: Residual OSA is common in older children, obesity, craniofacial risk, or more severe baseline disease. Very young children have higher surgical complication risk, and mild disease can sometimes justify watchful waiting.
